title: Few women who face violence go to court, dialogue hears as 16 days of activism begin
excerpt: At a Manusher Jonno Foundation dialogue, speakers said only about 7% of women abused by partners take legal action, and support services lack staff and pay.
content:
Very few women in Bangladesh who face violence take legal action, and those who do often do not get the help they need, speakers said at a national dialogue organised by Manusher Jonno Foundation (MJF) in Dhaka on Tuesday (24 November), Prothom Alo reported. The dialogue was held ahead of the 16 Days of Activism against gender-based violence, which begin today, Wednesday (25 November).

Speakers cited the 2024 Violence Against Women Survey by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) and UNFPA. In the survey's own release, BBS and the UN said 76% of women had experienced at least one form of intimate partner violence in their lifetime, 62% never told anyone, and 7.4% of survivors of partner violence took legal action. Prothom Alo reported the non-disclosure figure presented at the dialogue as 64%; Devlens has used the survey's published figure.

Citing research by the Supreme Court and BRAC, speakers said a sample of 4,040 cases settled in 46 tribunals in 32 districts between January and June 2025 had a conviction rate of 3%. About 70% of accused were acquitted, and cases took 1,370 days on average.

MJF executive director Shaheen Anam said women must stop hiding abuse and asked whether strategies to prevent violence had gone wrong. Physician and politician Tasnim Jara said staff of the 109 women's helpline, the 999 emergency service and One-Stop Crisis Centres are not paid regularly and are short-staffed, so survivors often get only information. Economist Selim Jahan said the state cannot avoid responsibility and called for disaggregated data.

UN Women country representative Gitanjali Singh said survivors' protection and access to justice must be ensured so offenders do not go unpunished. Representatives of the Swedish embassy and the EU delegation also spoke. MJF governing board chair Parveen Mahmud said awareness alone was not enough and the government must protect survivors and hold offenders to account.

Why it matters

The figures show a gap between prevalence and justice: most survivors stay silent, few go to court, and fewer see a conviction. Legal aid and GBV programmes run by NGOs depend on helplines, crisis centres and tribunals that speakers say are underfunded and slow.

What to watch

Government and donor announcements during the 16 days, which end on Human Rights Day on 10 December, and whether funding and staffing for the 109 helpline and One-Stop Crisis Centres are addressed.

Sources

  • United Nations Bangladesh: Three out of four women in Bangladesh experience violence: Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics survey, 15 October 2025
